sentences.text: Amargasaurus is distinctively characterized by two parallel rows of tall spines running down its neck and back, which are taller than those of any other known sauropod. This dinosaur was small for a sauropod, measuring 9 to 13 meters in length and weighing approximately 2.5 to 4 metric tons.

It had a shorter neck than most other sauropods, a trait common within the family Dicraeosauridae. The neck consisted of thirteen opisthocoelous cervical vertebrae that formed ball-and-socket joints with neighboring vertebrae.
Members of the Diplodocoidea, including Amargasaurus, had box-shaped snouts and narrow teeth restricted to the front of their jaws.

Amargasaurus was described by Salgado and Bonaparte in 1991. The only known skeleton, specimen MACN-N 15, was discovered in February 1984 by Guillermo Rougier during an expedition led by José Bonaparte.

This specimen is virtually complete, though it includes only a fragmentary skull. The discovery site is located in the La Amarga arroyo in the Picún Leufú Department of Neuquén Province, 70 km south of Zapala.

Amargasaurus probably fed at mid-height, based on the orientation of its inner ear and neck vertebrae articulation. Based on inner ear models, researchers suggested Amargasaurus held its snout at a downward angle of approximately 65 degrees relative to the horizontal.
Research suggests Amargasaurus had poorer hearing than other studied sauropods because its inner ear lagena was relatively short.

Amargasaurus is classified as a member of the family Dicraeosauridae within the order Sauropoda. It is classified within the family Dicraeosauridae, which is a clade inside the superfamily Diplodocoidea.
Amargasaurus was the first known dicraeosaurid dinosaur from the Cretaceous period.

Amargasaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically from the Barremian to the Aptian stages. Amargasaurus fossils come from the La Amarga Formation in the Neuquén Basin, dating to the Barremian and late Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
Amargasaurus lived between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago during the Barremian stage.

The exact function and life appearance of Amargasaurus's elongated vertebral spines remain unknown. Salgado and Bonaparte (1991) hypothesized that the spines served as defensive weapons because they tapered toward their tips. Some researchers have proposed that the spines supported two parallel skin sails for display. Jack Bailey (1997) suggested the spines resembled those of sail-bearing pelycosaurs and that Amargasaurus might have possessed a single skin sail.
